headline: Rage bait: the trick that turns your anger into money

sources.title: The Oxford Word of the Year 2025 is rage bait (Oxford University Press)
Don't get angry, but the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year is 'rage bait' (NPR)
Oxford University Press picks 'rage bait' as its word of the year (CBS News)
'Rage Bait' unveiled as Oxford's Word of the Year for 2025 (video, 6abc Philadelphia)

chunks.text: You see a post so wrong that your face gets hot. A cooking video that [[ruins]] a famous [[dish]] on purpose. An opinion nobody could truly believe. Before you type your [[furious]] reply, stop: it may be [[rage bait]], content made [[deliberately]] to {{stir up}} anger. The trick works because rage bait {{relies on}} one simple fact: angry people click, comment, and share more than happy ones.

verbs.correct: To cause strong feelings or trouble
verbs.wrong: To calm a group of people
verbs.why: You stir up anger, trouble, memories, or a whole crowd. Rage bait stirs up your feelings on purpose, because angry people click.

verbs.correct: To need something to work or succeed
verbs.wrong: To copy something step by step
verbs.why: You rely on your phone, your friends, or your paycheck. This whole business relies on one fact: anger gets more clicks than joy.

chunks.text: Here is how the game works. A creator posts something designed to feel [[unfair]] or completely wrong. Readers {{give in}} to the [[temptation]] to [[correct]] it, and soon hundreds of [[strangers]] {{pile on}} in the comments. Every reply pushes the post higher, so the crowd {{winds up}} paying the creator with the one thing he wanted: [[attention]]. The [[outrage]] is real, but the [[opinion]] often is not. Some rage baiters [[admit]] they do not believe a word of their own posts.

verbs.correct: To stop fighting a feeling or demand
verbs.wrong: To make a promise to yourself
verbs.why: People give in to temptation, pressure, and cravings. You promise not to reply, you read the post again, and you give in.

verbs.correct: To join many others in attacking
verbs.wrong: To leave a group one by one
verbs.why: When hundreds attack the same post or person, they pile on. It feels safe to pile on because everyone else is already doing it.

verbs.correct: To reach an end you did not plan
verbs.why: You wind up lost, awake at 3 a.m., or deep in an argument with a stranger. Nobody plans it, they just wind up there.

chunks.text: The word had a big year. In December 2025, dictionary experts at Oxford picked rage bait as their [[word of the year]], beating aura farming and biohack. More than 30,000 people voted, and use of the term [[tripled]] in just twelve months. The phrase {{caught on}} quickly, but the idea is older: it first appeared in an online [[forum]] back in 2002. The [[editors]] define rage bait as content built to cause anger and raise a site's [[traffic]] and [[engagement]]. Angry readers who {{call out}} the trick in the comments often just make it stronger.

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.why: Songs, slang, and trends catch on. This phrase caught on so fast it went from internet forums to the dictionary.

verbs.correct: To publicly say something is wrong
verbs.wrong: To whisper a secret to a friend
verbs.why: People call out lies, cheating, and fake stories. Creators who use rage bait are now called out by name, publicly.

chunks.text: So what should you do when a post [[makes your blood boil]]? Experts say the hardest step is to {{pass up}} the chance to tell a stranger he is wrong. Try to {{hold back}} your first hot reply until the anger cools, and ask a simple question: who [[profits]] from my anger? The [[storm]] around a rage bait post usually {{blows over}} in a day, but the views remain forever. If a post exists only to make you angry, the smartest answer is quiet: do not [[take the bait]], and just {{log off}}.

verbs.correct: To choose not to take a chance
verbs.wrong: To grab an offer with both hands
verbs.why: You pass up job offers, desserts, and chances. The hardest thing online is passing up the chance to correct a stranger.

verbs.correct: To keep a strong feeling inside
verbs.why: You hold back tears, laughter, or an angry reply. The advice here: hold your first comment back until the anger cools.

verbs.correct: To pass and be forgotten soon
verbs.why: Storms, scandals, and internet drama blow over. The outrage blows over in a day, but the creator keeps the views forever.

verbs.correct: To stop using an app or website
verbs.wrong: To create a new online account
verbs.why: You log off a website, an app, or a work computer. Sometimes the smartest reply to the internet is logging off.

Rage bait spreads faster than good news.
He posts rage bait and counts the comments.

wordDefs.def: On purpose, not by accident
ex: She deliberately left the door open.

He deliberately chose the hardest question.

wordDefs.def: A strong wish to do something unwise

ex: The unfair penalty caused national outrage.

wordDefs.def: A term picked to sum up the past year
ex: Editors announce the word of the year each December.

wordDefs.def: The number of visitors a website gets
ex: The blog's traffic doubled after the interview.

ex: The video's engagement surprised everyone.

wordDefs.def: To react exactly as a trick intended
ex: He teased her, and she took the bait.

wordDefs.def: Destroys or spoils something
ex: Salt ruins the taste if you add too much.

ex: The extra homework felt unfair.

ex: Do not share your address with strangers.

ex: He would not admit that he was lost.

wordDefs.def: People who choose and prepare published words
ex: The editors cut the story in half.

Editors checked every fact twice.

ex: He asked for advice on a car forum.

wordDefs.def: Became three times bigger
ex: The town's population tripled in ten years.
Ticket prices tripled after the final.

wordDefs.def: Makes you extremely angry
ex: Slow internet makes your blood boil.
That referee makes your blood boil.

wordDefs.def: Gains money or advantage from something
ex: The store profits from tourist season.

mainIdea.s: Rage bait, online content made on purpose to cause anger, was named word of the year after its use tripled. The article explains how it earns money and how to resist it.
mainIdea.why: Oxford picked the term in December 2025. Angry clicks raise traffic, and experts say the best answer is to log off.

mainIdea.s: Dictionary editors gave their 2025 prize to a term describing posts made to spread calm and kindness online. Use of that friendly phrase tripled in just twelve months.
mainIdea.why: Close, but rage bait is the opposite of friendly. It is built to stir up anger, and clicks turn that anger into money.

mainIdea.s: A famous chef lost his cooking show this winter after fans discovered that he ruined popular dishes on purpose. He says the angry comments have destroyed his whole career.
mainIdea.why: The ruined dish is only an example of rage bait. Nobody loses a show in the article.

tf.s: Rage bait relies on the fact that angry people click and share more
tf.why: That is the engine. Every furious reply pushes the post higher in the feed.

tf.s: Use of the term rage bait tripled in twelve months
tf.why: That growth helped it beat aura farming and biohack for word of the year.

tf.s: The idea of rage bait first appeared in 2025
tf.why: The term first appeared in an online forum back in 2002. Only the fame is new.

tf.s: Readers who pile on in the comments make the post weaker
tf.why: Every reply is fuel. The crowd winds up paying the creator with attention.

tf.s: Some rage baiters admit they do not believe their own posts
tf.why: The outrage they stir up is real, but the opinion often is not.

tf.s: Experts say the best response to rage bait is a long, angry reply
tf.why: They say to hold back, pass up the argument, and simply log off.
